title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner

paper.title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
paper.abstract:
Abstract. End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments.
Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail;
closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone.
Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward.
Our approach exploits this asymmetry by decoupling learning to drive and learning to plan from learning to see .
We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action Kullback-Leibler divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss.
Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on.
From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard , above every published method including DriveZero-Scale ( 57.1 57.1 ), and 95.5 95.5 PDMS on navtest , without human demonstrations.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: End-to-end autonomous driving maps raw sensor inputs ( e.g. , camera images) directly to control commands. Deep learning and large-scale driving data have made this approach widely adopted and continuously improved across benchmarks ( Bojarski et al., 2016 ; Codevilla et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ; Dauner et al., 2024a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . However, this progress relies on expensive standard pipelines that follow either of the two routes. The open-loop strategy draws its behavioral supervision from fleet logs: imitation copies logged human driving ( Codevilla et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ) , and open-loop reinforcement learning (RL) optimizes against logged trajectories ( Karkus et al., 2025 ) . These logs provide millions of multi-camera hours ( Caesar et al., 2020 ; Sun et al., 2020 ; Caesar et al., 2021 ) , yet safety-critical events (collisions, near-misses, recoveries, etc. ) remain vanishingly rare in natural driving: at NHTSA crash rates, a collision occurs only once every ∼ 16 {\sim}16 k driving hours ( National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 2025 ) , so logging a single rare event can easily cost over $1M in fleet operation alone ( Kelkar et al., 2025 ) . Each sub-route inherits this scarcity in its own way: imitation can only copy the actions the recorded drivers took, and open-loop RL never sees how other vehicles would have responded to the alternative actions it explores. Broadening interaction coverage with human data therefore demands ever more collection and curation. The closed-loop framework instead trains inside a photorealistic, sensor-rendering simulator ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ; Karkus et al., 2025 ) , where the policy experiences the consequences of its own actions. This interaction, however, costs rendering and a heavy vision-backbone forward pass at every step. Co-training multiple interacting agents multiplies these per-step costs, so most image-based closed-loop work instead trains the ego policy against scripted or log-replayed traffic, and the behavior distribution stays close to the logged or hand-designed content ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2022 ) . These costs confine this route to fine-tuning a pretrained imitation policy, as in Figure 1 , rather than pretraining driving competence from scratch. Recently, multi-agent self-play has risen as a promising alternative to offer the missing interaction: one shared policy controls every agent, so each policy improvement reshapes the traffic every other agent faces, and the interactive behavior co-evolves with the policy. Vectorized simulation makes this co-training highly efficient, executing millions of steps per second on commodity hardware ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2026 ; Seong et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Training requires only a basic definition of driving quality as per-step rewards: goal reaching, collision avoidance, comfort, and simple rule compliance. These rewards specify general driving objectives rather than separate rules for corner cases. The resulting interactions naturally produce the collisions, recoveries, yielding, negotiation, and overtaking that logged traffic seldom contains, all without expert trajectories or behavior-specific rewards. Despite its promise, however, self-play does not yield deployable end-to-end driving policies per se , as they observe vectorized scene state rather than raw sensors. Deploying these policies would require a two-stage perception stack that recovers their HD-map-style inputs from images. Such a stack demands high-quality perception, is sensitive to perception noise, and forfeits the co-optimization of a fully differentiable end-to-end model. As a result, it has mostly remained confined to traffic simulation rather than an end-to-end solution ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2026 ; Seong et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Konstantinidis et al., 2026 ; Ahmadi et al., 2026 ) . Ours Phase 1: learn to drive Phase 2: learn to plan Phase 3: learn to see Fleet logs human data Imitation pretraining Fine-tuning SFT / RL Final policy Conventional Figure 1 . Conventional training pipeline vs. our reinforcement-learning pretraining pipeline. Conventional recipes imitate fleet logs and fine-tune on curated demonstrations, logged trajectories, or rendered simulation. They therefore need human data or rendering at every stage. Phase 1 (top right) trains a self-play policy π θ \pi_{\theta} with proximal policy optimization (PPO) in a multi-agent vectorized simulator. Phase 2 (middle right) freezes the policy as the self-play teacher and distills its rollouts into a trajectory teacher that also outputs a planned trajectory; both teachers read vector state. Phase 3 (bottom right) aligns an image-conditioned student to either frozen teacher: the self-play teacher yields the closed-loop student, and the trajectory teacher yields the planning student. The student keeps the teacher’s ego encoder unchanged and is not aligned on it; only the teacher’s scene features (road and partner, plus traffic for the trajectory teacher) enter the structural loss. An action loss matches the teacher’s action distribution, while a structural loss matches its pairwise relationships among scenes; for the planning student, an L2 loss also matches the plan the trajectory teacher selects among 16 16 samples. Alignment uses paired (image, scene-state) frames; it needs neither demonstrations nor online rendering during training. Blue modules are trainable; outlined modules are frozen. In the blue DINOv3 + Adapter block, only the adapter trains; the backbone stays frozen. The trajectory head and the L2 loss apply to the planning student only. In this work, we unite the strengths of self-play and end-to-end driving in a paradigm that learns driving policies without expert demonstrations. Self-play learns driving competence without human demonstrations but consumes vector state; end-to-end recipes consume raw sensors but depend on human demonstrations, whose coverage of rare interactions is the very gap identified above. We bridge this gap by decoupling learning to drive and learning to plan from learning to see , and we never use logged demonstration trajectories as supervision. Figure 1 contrasts its three stages with the conventional workflow. In the first stage, we train a policy π θ \pi_{\theta} tabula rasa through multi-agent self-play in TerraZero ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , our vectorized driving simulator, in the spirit of GigaFlow ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ) . One parameter set controls every agent in every scene. The policy learns from the long-tail distribution of its own behavior and never imitates a human trajectory. The resulting policy is a strong planner, scoring 94.19 94.19 on nuPlan val14 and 70.87 70.87 on the interactive long-tail InterPlan suite, above every imitation-based planner we are aware of, and 0.632 0.632 human-similarity on WOSAC 2023, on par with the strongest learned sim agents. In the second stage, the policy becomes the self-play teacher, and a trajectory teacher learns to plan from its self-play rollouts. A closed-loop policy emits one action per step, but planning interfaces and pseudo closed-loop benchmarks score a multi-second trajectory. We therefore distill the realized futures of these rollouts into the trajectory teacher through a flow-matching head. Like the self-play teacher, it still reads vector state. In the third stage, we freeze either teacher and align a vision student to it: the self-play teacher yields the closed-loop student, and the trajectory teacher yields the planning student. The student retains the teacher’s head unchanged and learns encoders that produce its scene features for road elements and surrounding agents from images instead of vector states; these encoders pair a pretrained vision backbone ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) with learned adapters supervised by paired (image, scene-state) frames of the same scene. The teacher’s per-state action distribution trains the student to choose the same actions. A feature-level structural loss preserves the teacher’s pairwise similarities among scene features, following the empirical finding that the teacher’s features are low-rank and redundant (§ 3.5 ). For the planning student, a trajectory loss also matches the plan the trajectory teacher selects among 16 16 samples, so the student learns the selection and needs none at test time. The closed-loop and planning students are two interfaces of one self-play teacher, and neither sees a human trajectory. Our framework preserves the naturalistic driving competence learned through self-play. On photorealistic closed-loop benchmarks, the closed-loop student attains an aggregate HD-Score of 0.548 0.548 , exceeding every published end-to-end baseline on every HUGSim dataset split (Table 1 ). Likewise, on NAVSIM, the planning student reaches 59.4 59.4 EPDMS on the NAVSIMv2 navhard split, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale ( 57.1 57.1 ), and 95.5 95.5 PDMS on the NAVSIMv1 navtest split, above every published sensor-based method (Table 2 ). TerraTransfer++ extends our earlier TerraTransfer report ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) with trajectory distillation, the second stage. The cost of learning to drive moves upstream into self-play. This one-time compute is efficient and reusable. The self-play policy is trained in 96 hours on 16 A100 GPUs, covering over 2.4B kilometers of simulated driving without human demonstrations. It can then supervise a range of vision frontends, alignment datasets, sensor stacks, and downstream specializations. During alignment, the vision encoder’s only teacher signals are the frozen head’s per-state action distribution, the teacher’s scene-feature relations, and, for the planning student, the trajectory teacher’s selected plan; all three derive from the self-play teacher’s behavior and are computed on a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames. No expert behavior is required anywhere. Any retained perception labels are policy-agnostic and reusable across frontends. They are obtainable offline through auto-labeling, which separates this requirement from the demonstration-collection burden of behavior cloning. In our case, the encoder is aligned over 1.83 1.83 M paired nuPlan frames plus 300 300 K HUGSim domain-adaptation frames on 8 A100 GPUs in 10 hours. The nuPlan paired frames are logged real camera images and the domain-adaptation frames are rendered once offline, so training needs no online rendering; rendering in the loop would be roughly 6,000 × 6{,}000\times slower than vector rollout ( 175 175 k vs. 30 30 fps across all cameras). We make the following contributions: • A novel demonstration-free paradigm for learning end-to-end driving policies. A policy π θ \pi_{\theta} first learns to drive through multi-agent self-play in a vectorized simulator. Its per-state action distributions then supervise encoders that produce the policy’s scene features from images, with no logged-trajectory supervision at any stage. • Trajectory distillation from self-play. A flow-matching trajectory teacher learns the realized futures of the self-play teacher’s rollouts, and the same alignment recipe plus a loss on the teacher’s selected plan transfers it to a camera-only planner (§ 2.3 and § 2.4 ). The planner reaches 59.4 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2 navhard , above every published method including DriveZero-Scale ( 57.1 57.1 ), and 95.5 95.5 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 navtest , above every published sensor-based method (Table 2 ). • A feature-level structural alignment mechanism. We align the encoder directly with the teacher’s pooled scene features instead of cascading reconstruction and detection. A batch-relational low-rank structural loss matches the pairwise scene similarities induced by the teacher. • Demonstration-free closed-loop driving beyond published imitation-based end-to-end methods. On photorealistic closed-loop scenarios in HUGSim, the camera-based closed-loop student, aligned to a teacher that never observed a human demonstration, outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method (Table 1 ).

sections.heading: 2. Method
sections.text: We first train a vector-state teacher through self-play, then distill its rollouts into a trajectory teacher that also plans, and finally align a vision student to either teacher with structural and action losses.

sections.heading: 2.1. TerraZero: Self-Play Vectorized Simulator
sections.text: Self-play runs in TerraZero ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , a vectorized driving simulator that compiles nuPlan high-definition (HD) maps into static lane topology, lane boundaries, and drivable-area geometry. Training uses no nuPlan logged trajectories, logged agent initial states, logged goals, human actions, or replayed traffic. Instead, controlled vehicles spawn procedurally from lane centerlines through rejection sampling. This procedure produces collision-free, drivable initial scenes. Each controlled vehicle receives a procedural goal between 20 20 and 100 100 m ahead along the reachable lane graph. Reaching a goal triggers another sample from the same topology. The simulator also places vulnerable road users and static obstacles as scene context. The learned policy controls vehicles only. Appendix A.1.1 gives the complete environment and training configuration. At each 0.1 0.1 s step, a vehicle observes its ego kinematics and goal signal, nearby road polylines and traffic controls, and neighboring scene entities. Each entity includes relative pose, velocity, heading, size, type, and validity. These three input groups become the ego, road, and partner streams used by the teacher below. Appendix A.1.2 specifies the observation vectors. Appendices A.1.3 – A.1.5 detail rewards and dynamics.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We pretrain a driving policy π θ \pi_{\theta} through self-play in TerraZero. A single set of parameters θ \theta controls all agents in every scene. We pool their transitions into one on-policy buffer. Each agent’s “surrounding traffic” consists of other instances of the current policy. The multi-agent interaction distribution therefore evolves with the policy itself.

sections.text: Self-play supplies the experience; the reward defines what counts as good behavior within it. We define the per-step reward R t ( n ) R^{(n)}_{t} for agent n n as a weighted sum of K K driving-quality terms: (3) R t ( n ) = ∑ k = 1 K w k ( n ) ⋅ r t ( k ) ​ ( o t ( n ) , a t ( n ) ) . R^{(n)}_{t}\;=\;\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{K}w^{(n)}_{k}\cdot r^{(k)}_{t}\!\big(o^{(n)}_{t},\,a^{(n)}_{t}\big). The terms measure goal-reaching, collision, comfort, lane alignment, lane centering, velocity, traffic-rule compliance, and related driving qualities (see Appendix A.1.3 ). Following the domain-randomization scheme of GigaFlow ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ) , we resample the weights w k ( n ) ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( w k min , w k max ) w^{(n)}_{k}\sim\mathcal{U}(w_{k}^{\min},w_{k}^{\max}) for each agent and episode. We include the sampled weights in the policy’s ego observation o t e o^{e}_{t} . This conditioning trains a single π θ \pi_{\theta} to act consistently across a continuum of driver preferences.

sections.heading: 2.3. Trajectory Distillation
sections.text: The frozen teacher π θ T \pi^{T}_{\theta} emits one action per step but publishes no planned trajectory, which planning interfaces and pseudo closed-loop protocols require. We therefore give it a second interface: we distill its rollouts into a trajectory teacher that also outputs a plan (Phase 2 of Fig. 1 ). Both teachers read privileged vector state; § 2.4 turns either into a vision policy.

sections.heading: Target construction.
sections.text: For each frame of a self-play rollout, the trajectory target is the realized future of π θ T \pi^{T}_{\theta} , not a logged human trajectory. We record the next 80 80 ego poses at the native 10 10 Hz control rate ( 8 8 s), each expressed in the current ego frame as forward offset, lateral offset, and heading change, and standardize every timestep and dimension with dataset statistics. A pose is masked out of the loss once the future leaves the rollout horizon or the route switches. For NAVSIM, the predicted plan is decimated to the 2 2 Hz, 4 4 s ( 8 8 -pose) protocol format ( Dauner et al., 2024b ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . One hour of self-play rollouts on 64 64 GPUs yields 600 600 M such 8 8 s, 10 10 Hz trajectories for trajectory distillation.

sections.heading: Trajectory teacher.
sections.text: The trajectory teacher is a transformer policy of 11.2 11.2 M parameters over the same vector observation, trained on the actions and realized futures of π θ T \pi^{T}_{\theta} . Entity encoders. Unlike π θ T \pi^{T}_{\theta} , whose road stream also carries the traffic controls, the trajectory teacher gives partner, road, and traffic-control entities each their own encoder. An entity token is the sum of an MLP over its features, a Fourier encoding of its relative position, and a type embedding ( d = 128 d=128 ). Masked self-attention runs over the tokens of each type ( 2 2 layers for partners and roads, 1 1 for traffic controls). Learned queries then cross-attend to the tokens, and a linear projection with layer normalization yields the per-type latent tokens: 8 8 road latents z r ∈ ℝ 8 × 64 z^{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{8\times 64} , 8 8 partner latents z p ∈ ℝ 8 × 64 z^{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{8\times 64} , and 4 4 traffic latents z c ∈ ℝ 4 × 64 z^{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 64} . The latents are projected to d = 256 d=256 and tagged with a type embedding. Together with the ego token, they form 21 21 tokens, which 3 3 self-attention layers fuse into F ∈ ℝ 21 × 256 F\in\mathbb{R}^{21\times 256} . Action head. A flow-matching denoiser ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) operates on the 80 80 waypoint tokens. Each of its 4 4 blocks applies self-attention over waypoints, cross-attention to F F , and an MLP. Every block is modulated by adaptive layer normalization on the flow time t t and e e . sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: The alignment applies to either frozen teacher (Phase 3 of Fig. 1 ). We describe it for π θ T \pi^{T}_{\theta} , which yields the closed-loop student, and turn to the trajectory teacher at the end of this section. The self-play teacher supplies per-frame supervision. The student keeps the teacher’s frozen policy head, comprising the shared MLP and actor head. It also keeps the frozen ego encoder E ego E_{\text{ego}} . The student replaces only its own road and partner encoders with image-conditioned counterparts E r vis , E p vis E^{\text{vis}}_{r},E^{\text{vis}}_{p} . Given an image I t I_{t} paired with the teacher’s vector observation o t o_{t} , the student and teacher features are (6) ( f t r , f t p ) = ( E r vis ​ ( I t ) , E p vis ​ ( I t ) ) , ( f ^ t r , f ^ t p ) = ( E r ​ ( 𝒪 t r ) , E p ​ ( 𝒪 t p ) ) . \big(f^{r}_{t},\,f^{p}_{t}\big)=\big(E^{\text{vis}}_{r}(I_{t}),\,E^{\text{vis}}_{p}(I_{t})\big),\qquad\big(\hat{f}^{r}_{t},\,\hat{f}^{p}_{t}\big)=\big(E_{r}(\mathcal{O}^{r}_{t}),\,E_{p}(\mathcal{O}^{p}_{t})\big). The frozen DeepSets encoders E r , E p E_{r},E_{p} from Eq. 1 produce the teacher features f ^ t r , f ^ t p \hat{f}^{r}_{t},\hat{f}^{p}_{t} , exactly as during self-play. The two vision encoders share a single frozen DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) backbone and differ only in their adapters: E r vis E^{\text{vis}}_{r} and E p vis E^{\text{vis}}_{p} apply separate linear adapters to the same backbone features, producing the road and partner features f t r , f t p f^{r}_{t},f^{p}_{t} (Fig. 1 ). Under a fixed alignment recipe, this backbone gives the strongest closed-loop score among the alternatives we ablate (Appendix B.2 ). The student receives camera images together with the ego vector, whose goal signal is the endpoint of the logged ego trajectory, whereas the teacher additionally receives vector road and partner state. A possible bridge is a cascade : a perception module recovers the teacher’s vector inputs (bounding boxes, lane polylines, and partner kinematics) from the image, and the frozen teacher then consumes these recovered inputs. We avoid this cascade for two reasons. First, it is not end-to-end differentiable: the perception module trains on surrogate detection objectives, so no gradient couples its errors to the driving quality that the frozen head serves, and the perception stage makes any future end-to-end post-training of the policy harder. Second, the teacher trains on clean simulator state and is sensitive to input noise; a perception module that imperfectly recovers that state degrades the head it feeds. We supervise the student with two complementary objectives. The action loss aligns policy distributions, but a softmax is coarse: different feature configurations can yield the same action logits. The structural loss matches feature relations in the informative low-rank subspace of § 3.5 . It preserves how the teacher arranges scenes relative to one another, but its pairwise angles are invariant to rotations and shifts, so it alone cannot ensure that the frozen head maps features to the right actions. Together, the action loss anchors actions and the structural loss shapes scene geometry.

sections.heading: Action alignment.
sections.text: Following classical distillation ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , we match the student’s policy distribution to the teacher’s by forward KL divergence, (7) ℒ act = KL ( π T ( ⋅ ∣ o t ) ∥ π S ( ⋅ ∣ I t , o t e ) ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{act}}\;=\;\mathrm{KL}\!\big(\pi^{T}(\cdot\mid o_{t})\;\|\;\pi^{S}(\cdot\mid I_{t},o^{e}_{t})\big). We match the full distribution rather than the sampled action: the distribution carries the teacher’s uncertainty across the action set, so near-ambiguous scenes teach the student the same ambiguity instead of a single arbitrary choice. This policy-level objective provides a global consistency signal. Minimizing it encourages the student’s policy distribution to approach the teacher’s, regardless of how the student represents road and partner features.

sections.heading: Structural alignment.
sections.text: The structural loss matches scene geometry: scenes the teacher treats as alike should remain alike for the student. This relational target complements the action loss rather than adding a second coordinate-regression objective. The informative variation in the teacher’s features is sharply low-rank, as shown in § 3.5 . Matching every coordinate would also force the student to fit the structureless tail. An optimal low-rank denoiser discards these low-variance directions as noise ( Gavish and Donoho, 2014 ) . We call the span of the informative directions the teacher principal subspace and align features only within it. sections.heading: Trajectory student.
sections.text: Replacing π θ T \pi^{T}_{\theta} with the trajectory teacher of § 2.3 in the same recipe yields the planning student, which we call the trajectory student. A frozen DINOv3 backbone with lightweight adapters predicts the 20 20 per-type latent tokens ( z r , z p , z c ) (z^{r},z^{p},z^{c}) from the image, and the action and structural losses align them with the trajectory teacher’s latents: ℒ act \mathcal{L}_{\text{act}} is the KL divergence to the trajectory teacher’s action head, and ℒ struct \mathcal{L}_{\text{struct}} is applied per type to the flattened latents, with λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 . A third loss, ℒ traj \mathcal{L}_{\text{traj}} , distills the teacher’s selected plan. On navtrain , the trajectory teacher samples 16 16 plans per frame and keeps the best under the constant-velocity selection of § 3.1 , which reads ground-truth agent states. The frozen trajectory head samples a plan from the student’s latents, and ℒ traj \mathcal{L}_{\text{traj}} is the L2 distance between this plan and the selected teacher plan over all 80 80 waypoints. It is added to ℒ align \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} with weight 1 1 . The ego encoder, fusion layers, and both heads stay frozen and consume the predicted latents; the ego embedding is computed from the ego state and is never aligned. At inference, the student samples a single plan and performs no selection.

sections.heading: 3. Experiments
sections.text: We test one claim: vision policies distilled from a self-play teacher can drive competitively in closed loop and plan competitively in pseudo closed loop. No training stage touches a logged human trajectory. We first define the setup and the two scorers (§ 3.1 ) and present the self-play teacher that anchors the pipeline (§ 3.2 ); the teacher sets the reference level. We then compare the student and the teacher against end-to-end baselines on every HUGSim split and against concurrent self-play-to-pixel systems on their 345 345 -scenario protocol (§ 3.3 ), and compare the trajectory student against published planners on NAVSIM (§ 3.4 ); the two students are the main results. Next, the insights and ablations of § 3.5 show that, under matched data and compute, self-play alignment outperforms imitation and a modular cascade: the training paradigm sets the score, both alignment losses are necessary and nearly lossless, and the low-rank structural target is read from the teacher’s spectrum rather than tuned. The appendix details the setup of the rank ablation (Appendix B.1 ) and ablates the vision backbone (Appendix B.2 ).

sections.heading: 3.1. Setup
sections.text: We evaluate on all 436 436 scenarios of HUGSim ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , a photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark, spanning its four dataset splits (nuScenes 88 88 , PandaSet 127 127 , KITTI-360 113 113 , Waymo 108 108 ), each divided into Easy, Medium, Hard, and Extreme tiers. On HUGSim we report two scores throughout: the closed-loop (CL) HD-Score, which scores the realized rollout, and HUGSim’s native scorer, which scores a planned trajectory. Our single-step controller replans at each step, emitting one immediate jerk action that we Euler-integrate into HUGSim’s bicycle-model control signals in causal closed form, without a second dynamics model (Appendix A.1.5 specifies the conversion). The closed-loop scorer executes only this first action per step and scores the resulting rollout. The native scorer, in contrast, needs a full trajectory that our controller does not publish, so we give it the decel stand-in plan: the realized first step followed by a comfort-bounded stop. Appendix A.2 defines both scorers in detail; Appendix A.3 reports per-split, per-tier subscores for the teacher and the student (baselines appear in Table 1 ). Absolute score magnitudes are not directly comparable across dataset splits: PandaSet ships no HD vector map, so its scorer evaluates DAC against a per-scene 3D ground point cloud and R c R_{c} against the native centerline.

sections.heading: Alignment data.
sections.text: The paired dataset only teaches the vision frontend to reproduce the frozen teacher’s behavior. The headline run uses ≈ 1.83 \approx\!1.83 M paired (image, scene-state) frames from nuPlan ( Caesar et al., 2021 ) : 7,129 7{,}129 shards of 256 256 frames, or ∼ \sim 51 hours at 10 10 Hz. At each frame, the target is the teacher’s action distribution on the reconstructed scene. The logged ego trajectory is never used as a target; only its endpoint enters the student’s ego vector as the goal signal (§ 2.4 ). Perception labels are policy-agnostic and can be obtained offline, so this supervision is decoupled from expert behavior rather than strictly weaker than demonstration collection. Beyond the nuPlan corpus, we sample 300 300 K paired frames in total from the HUGSim reconstructions of the four evaluation splits ( ∼ \sim 75K per split) for domain adaptation, following the real-world-simulation practice of SimScale ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . These synthetic frames are rendered from the evaluation scenes themselves but cover only 10 % 10\% of their total route length. The paradigm ablation and the privileged probe in § 3.5 use the nuPlan frames alone; the rank and backbone ablations use the headline data, including the domain-adaptation frames. The trajectory student of § 3.4 is aligned on NAVSIM navtrain only.

sections.heading: Teacher plans on NAVSIM.
sections.text: The NAVSIM protocol of § 3.4 scores a 4 4 s plan, which we take from the trajectory teacher of § 2.3 . In each scene, its flow-matching head samples 16 16 trajectories from 16 16 different noise draws, which yields 16 16 candidate plans. We then forecast the other agents over the same horizon and keep the candidate that scores best on collision, time-to-collision (TTC), and progress against that forecast. The default teacher forecasts the agents by constant-velocity extrapolation; the IDM-selection variant forecasts them with the intelligent driver model ( Treiber et al., 2000 ) . We apply this procedure at both navhard stages. Like the teacher itself, selection reads ground-truth agent states, so both teacher rows of Table 2 are privileged references.

sections.heading: 3.2. Teacher Closed-Loop Results
sections.text: Before vision alignment, the self-play teacher outscores every published imitation-based planner on the nuPlan-based planning benchmarks whose maps it trains on. It reaches 94.19 94.19 on the nuPlan val14 suite ( Caesar et al., 2021 ) , compared with 92.28 92.28 for the best prior imitation planner. On the interactive long-tail InterPlan suite ( Hallgarten et al., 2024 ) , it reaches 70.87 70.87 , compared with 63.66 63.66 . The teacher’s exported rollouts also score 0.632 0.632 on the WOSAC 2023 human-likeness benchmark ( Montali et al., 2023 ) , within 0.09 0.09 of the 0.722 0.722 logged-oracle reference and on par with the strongest learned sim agents, without observing a human demonstration. The teacher also transfers beyond its nuPlan training maps. It reaches an aggregate closed-loop HD-Score of 0.647 0.647 on the HUGSim nuScenes split, 0.710 0.710 on Waymo, 0.554 0.554 on PandaSet, and 0.363 0.363 on KITTI-360, across 436 436 scenarios ( 0.562 0.562 overall; Table 7 ). For KITTI-360, whose lanes and road edges we re-derive from the reconstruction point cloud, the teacher reads the re-derived edges. Appendix A.3 reports the per-tier closed-loop breakdowns. These transfer results position the teacher as a privileged reference. It drives from vectorized scene state on HD maps: nuScenes and Waymo ship their own, and we generate them for KITTI-360 and PandaSet as teacher inputs.

sections.heading: Comparison with concurrent self-play-to-pixel systems.
sections.text: Two concurrent self-play-to-pixel systems report results on HUGSim: GigaPixel ( Rowe et al., 2026 ) trains in a dedicated bounding-box renderer and reaches a native HD-Score of 0.385 0.385 ; DriveZero ( He et al., 2026 ) regresses teacher rollouts collected on real log-initialized worlds and reaches 0.466 0.466 . Both were evaluated on the pre-challenge 345 345 -scenario protocol of Kirby et al. (2026) , which the current 436 436 -scenario release later superseded; their checkpoints are not public, so we re-evaluate our system on the same 345 345 scenarios with HUGSim’s native scorer (Figure 2 ). The teacher reaches 0.527 0.527 and the student 0.518 0.518 , exceeding both systems. Our native scores use the decel stand-in plan, which satisfies the comfort bounds by construction, whereas GigaPixel and DriveZero are scored on the plans their policies output. The training loops differ as well: GigaPixel keeps a renderer in its loop, and DriveZero keeps per-scene teacher rollouts, whereas our alignment consumes the frozen teacher’s action distributions and scene-feature relations on fixed paired frames: it needs no rendering in the loop and no teacher rollouts during alignment (the 300 300 K domain-adaptation frames are rendered once, offline). sections.heading: Extreme-tier failure mode.
sections.text: The student’s weakest tier is Extreme ( 0.162 0.162 closed-loop, 0.137 0.137 native, pooled over all splits), where even the teacher reference manages only 0.158 0.158 and 0.136 0.136 , and baselines retain an edge on parts of this tier: ECO on PandaSet, KITTI-360, and Waymo under the closed-loop scorer and on nuScenes and Waymo under the native scorer, and the imitation-trained baselines on KITTI-360 under both. Its adversarial scenarios are partly implausible (Figure 3 ): the other agents collide with the ego regardless of what the ego does, so a policy that just accelerates and drives straight, never reacting, already scores 0.227 0.227 closed-loop, above every reactive policy. The student, like the teacher it is aligned to, instead waits for the oncoming vehicle as a human driver would and sacrifices route completion. The resulting low R c R_{c} reduces aggregate HD-Score on this tier (Appendix A.3 ). The tier thus punishes exactly the reactive behavior we want. Figure 3 . Visually implausible extreme-tier scenarios. Some HUGSim Extreme scenarios begin from implausible configurations: other views are occluded, and vehicles appear to pass through one another. Configurations like these trigger the student’s conservative yielding, which sacrifices route completion and pulls the Extreme scores of Table 1 down for every method.

sections.heading: 3.5. Insights and Ablations
sections.text: Together, § 3.3 and § 3.4 show that one alignment recipe carries the self-play teacher’s competence into both students. The insights and ablations below study that recipe on the closed-loop student of § 2.4 .

sections.heading: The teacher’s features are low-rank.
sections.text: Figure 4 shows where the teacher’s structure lives. The road spectrum concentrates 80 % 80\% of its energy in the first 9 9 directions, the partner spectrum in the first 13 13 of 64 64 . The energy of direction i i is its squared singular value σ i 2 \sigma_{i}^{2} , so the cumulative fraction ∑ j ≤ i σ j 2 / ∑ j σ j 2 \sum_{j\leq i}\sigma_{j}^{2}/\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}^{2} is the variance explained by the first i i directions. The structural loss therefore matches pairwise similarities only within these dominant subspaces, and the cutoffs are read from the spectrum rather than tuned. We expect two failure modes when the truncation moves either way. A rank set too low discards directions that carry real structure, so the loss stops constraining the student where constraint matters. A rank set too high pulls in the weakly structured tail, whose variation the image cannot explain, so the encoder is dragged toward a target it cannot identify. The ablation in Table 3 bears both expectations out: performance peaks at the spectrum-predicted cutoff and drops on either side, most at full coordinates. Figure 4 . sections.heading: The losses are nearly lossless.
sections.text: The two losses are the only channel through which the teacher reaches the student. If they failed to express some of the teacher’s competence, no encoder, however perfect, could recover the missing part. We therefore first quantify the cost of the objective itself. A privileged probe provides the measurement. The probe replaces the vision encoders with freshly initialized encoders of the teacher’s own architecture, the two DeepSets of § 2.2 , which consume the privileged vector observation o t o_{t} instead of images. We train it with the same losses on the same nuPlan paired frames, without the HUGSim domain-adaptation frames, and the frozen head and the teacher’s structural definition remain untouched. The probe therefore differs from the teacher in one variable only: its encoders are trained, not inherited. Two paired comparisons read the result. On the nuScenes split, the probe reaches 0.645 0.645 CL HD-Score against the teacher’s 0.647 0.647 : with identical vector inputs, the gap of 0.002 0.002 is negligible, so the alignment objective itself costs almost nothing. The camera student trained on the same nuPlan frames (Table 4 ) reaches 0.574 0.574 against the probe’s 0.645 0.645 : with an identical objective and identical data, the gap of 0.071 0.071 combines the cost of perception with the nuPlan-to-HUGSim domain gap. Adding the 300 300 K HUGSim domain-adaptation frames raises the headline student to 0.636 0.636 , within 0.009 0.009 of the probe. sections.heading: 4. Related Work
sections.text: Most end-to-end driving policies imitate logged human driving ( Codevilla et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) . However, driving competence can also be learned without human demonstrations through multi-agent self-play in vector-state simulators such as GigaFlow ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ) , TerraZero ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , and PufferDrive ( Cornelisse et al., 2025 ) . This raises the question of how to bring the resulting competence to camera-based policies. Several systems pursue this goal along two routes. The first route learns to drive in vector state and then transfers the behavior to images. Concurrent with our work, GigaPixel ( Rowe et al., 2026 ) distills its vector-state teacher into a pixel-based student through DAgger in a bounding-box renderer, then freezes that student’s head to adapt perception to real images. DriveZero ( He et al., 2026 ) instead trains a separate student planner, supervised by trajectories that a PPO teacher rolls out from logged frames. Although their transfer procedures differ, neither reuses the teacher’s policy head. The second route learns the behavior directly in image space, skipping the vector-state teacher. Pictura ( Yin et al., 2026 ) , also concurrent, renders each agent’s egocentric view at every self-play step and trains policies from these non-photorealistic perspective images. Cheap rendering scales the interaction, but the resulting policies remain in the renderer’s domain; a policy that consumes real camera images still requires a further training stage. Photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting simulators close this visual gap, but rendering every rollout at photorealistic quality is costly, so works like RAD ( Gao et al., 2025 ) and World Engine ( Li et al., 2026b ) use them only to post-train imitation-pretrained image policies rather than to learn driving from scratch. We take the first route, but retain the policy head learned through vector-state self-play and train encoders that produce its scene features from images instead of vector state. RAP ( Feng et al., 2026 ) likewise pairs lightweight rasterization with feature alignment, but applies them to imitation learning: it rasterizes counterfactual views from annotated logs and aligns raster features to real ones, whereas our alignment transfers the decisions of a self-play teacher. Concretely, on fixed paired (image, scene-state) frames we compute action-distribution targets per state and feature-relation targets across the batch, and, for the planning student, plan targets from the frozen trajectory head. Because these frames are fixed, alignment requires neither online rendering nor teacher rollouts.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: Our closed-loop and planning results support a simple three-stage recipe: learn driving behavior through multi-agent self-play, distill it into a trajectory teacher that also plans, and align vision students to either teacher for control and for planning. We train a self-play policy in TerraZero, our vectorized simulator, freeze it as the teacher, distill its rollouts into a trajectory teacher, and train vision frontends that produce each teacher’s scene features from paired (image, scene-state) frames. No stage trains against logged ego trajectories: the teachers’ behavior comes from self-play, and the alignment targets come from the frozen heads the students reuse. In the tested scenarios, the teacher outperforms imitation-trained pipelines, and the aligned vision policy retains most of that competence. The same teacher also yields a planner: the trajectory student reaches 59.4 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard , above every published method, and 95.5 95.5 PDMS on navtest , within 0.4 0.4 points of the privileged best-of- 16 16 trajectory teacher. Imitation can only replay maneuvers that a fleet log recorded, so its coverage of rare events is capped by what happened to occur; self-play generates collisions, recoveries, and negotiations on demand. We still use what the fleet log sees, but no longer what it does. In our matched-data comparison, self-play pretraining is therefore a stronger alternative to imitation-based pretraining for learning driving behavior, while imitation remains useful for visual cues unavailable in bounding-box state, such as brake lights and hand signals. Two extensions follow directly from this design. The teacher may base decisions on occluded agents that the camera cannot observe. Paired-frame alignment does not remove this gap; the privileged probe bounds the total perception cost (§ 3.5 ), but we have not separated the occlusion component from other perception errors. LEAD ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ) studies the asymmetry directly, Pictura ( Yin et al., 2026 ) sidesteps it by learning to drive from the rendered image itself, and belief-aware privileged distillation ( Haklidir, 2026 ) adapts the teacher’s guidance to what the student can observe. It is natural to extend the self-play training and distillation to these methods. Alignment also draws from nuPlan logs and reconstructed scenes, so it rarely encounters severe weather, unusual times of day, or rare scenario geometries. Controllable scene generation offers a way out: video world models such as DriveDreamer ( Wang et al., 2024 ) generate the image side of our pairs, Scenario Dreamer ( Rowe et al., 2025 ) produces the scene-state side as vectorized latents, and InfiniCube ( Lu et al., 2025b ) and SCube ( Huang et al., 2024 ) synthesize street scenes beyond the recorded weather and time of day. Pairing such generators with the self-play teacher would let both sides of the alignment come from procedurally controlled worlds.

sections.heading: Environment setup.
sections.text: Self-play training runs in TerraZero, the TerraZero vectorized driving simulator, and uses nuPlan HD maps as map geometry only. We compile nuPlan map geometry into simulator binaries and use lane topology, lane boundaries, and drivable-area polygons as static scene context; we do not use nuPlan logged trajectories, logged agent initial states, logged goals, human actions, or replayed traffic as training supervision. Controlled vehicles are spawned procedurally from lane centerlines by rejection sampling, so the initial scene is collision-free and drivable. The learned policy controls vehicles only; the simulator also procedurally places vulnerable road users and static obstacles as scene context, but these entities are not trained policies. Goals are also procedural. For each spawned vehicle, the simulator samples a target distance between 20 20 and 100 100 m and walks forward along the HD-map lane graph, selecting reachable lane successors and filtering candidates by connectivity and heading consistency. When a vehicle reaches its current goal, a new reachable goal is sampled from the same topology; no destination is taken from a log.

sections.heading: RL algorithm.
sections.text: The teacher is trained as a decentralized policy with PPO. We use V-trace-corrected GAE ( γ = 0.99 \gamma=0.99 , λ GAE = 0.95 \lambda_{\text{GAE}}=0.95 ), clipped PPO with clip coefficient 0.2 0.2 , entropy coefficient 0.01 0.01 , value coefficient 0.5 0.5 , Adam with an annealed 5 × 10 − 4 5{\times}10^{-4} learning rate, and bfloat16 mixed precision. The reference teacher run was trained on 16 16 A100 GPUs, with approximately 3 3 M cumulative agent steps/s throughput.

sections.heading: A.1.2. Observations
sections.text: At each simulator step ( Δ ​ t = 0.1 \Delta t=0.1 s), a controlled vehicle observes three groups of inputs matching the policy factorization in Eq. 1 : an ego vector, a variable-size set of road elements, and a variable-size set of nearby partners. The ego vector contains the vehicle kinematic state ( x , y , θ , v , a long , a lat , ϕ ) (x,y,\theta,v,a_{\text{long}},a_{\text{lat}},\phi) in the ego frame, the current navigation/goal signal, the sampled vehicle geometry and dynamics coefficients, and the per-episode reward-weight vector. Road observations encode nearby lane and boundary polylines and traffic controls (traffic lights and stop signs) relative to the ego frame. Partner observations encode neighboring scene entities by relative pose, velocity, heading, size, type, and validity masks. The road and partner sets are pooled by the DeepSets encoders described in § 2.2 .

sections.heading: A.1.4. Vehicle Dynamics
sections.text: We use the jerk-actuated bicycle dynamics and the discrete 12 12 -action longitudinal/lateral jerk grid from the vehicle branch of Cusumano-Towner et al. (2025) . As in that setup, each controlled vehicle maintains pose, speed, longitudinal and lateral acceleration, and steering state; selected jerk actions are integrated into accelerations, speed, steering, and finally pose using the simulator time step. Our dynamics setup differs from Cusumano-Towner et al. (2025) in three ways. First, because the learned policy controls vehicles only, dynamics randomization is restricted to passenger-car-sized bodies rather than the broader road-user size range used in that work: (11) length ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 3.5 , 5.5 ) ​ m , width ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 1.5 , 2.5 ) ​ m , height ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 1.2 , 2.0 ) ​ m . \textit{length}\sim\mathcal{U}(3.5,5.5)\,\mathrm{m},\qquad\textit{width}\sim\mathcal{U}(1.5,2.5)\,\mathrm{m},\qquad\textit{height}\sim\mathcal{U}(1.2,2.0)\,\mathrm{m}. Second, at every episode reset each vehicle samples the scalar dynamics coefficients (12) C throttle , C steer , C acc , C vel ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0.5 , 1.5 ) , C_{\text{throttle}},C_{\text{steer}},C_{\text{acc}},C_{\text{vel}}\sim\mathcal{U}(0.5,1.5), rather than the mixed-uniform coefficient distributions in Cusumano-Towner et al. (2025) . These coefficients and the sampled vehicle dimensions are included in the ego observation so the policy can condition on the vehicle it is controlling. Third, we run self-play with simulator step Δ ​ t = 0.1 \Delta t=0.1 s, which improves closed-loop reactivity and matches the control rate used by the student vision policy.

sections.heading: A.2. Closed-Loop HD-Score
sections.text: The native HUGSim ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) HD-Score is not well designed for closed-loop evaluation: it scores the policy’s planned future trajectory rather than the path the ego actually drives. 1 1 1 Throughout this appendix, the native HD-Score denotes the public HUGSim scorer sim/utils/score_calculator.py (repository hyzhou404/HUGSIM , commit 62c690d , 2025-11-08; https://github.com/hyzhou404/HUGSIM ), whose calculate() routine is the scoring entry point we benchmark against; all statements about native behavior below are taken from it. This is a legacy of the open-loop NAVSIM-style protocol ( Dauner et al., 2024a ) it was written for, where each keyframe carries a multi-second planned trajectory and the metric never has to commit to what is executed. But what we want to measure is closed-loop driving quality, which lives in the realized rollout trajectory, not in a plan the policy may never follow—and our single-step policy emits no multi-second plan to begin with. We therefore introduce a closed-loop variant of the HD-Score (used in § 3.1 ) that scores the realized rollout directly: we keep the aggregation formula, the no-collision (NC) and drivable-area-compliance (DAC) subscores, and the route-completion term ( R c R_{c} ) unchanged, and redefine the time-to-collision (TTC) and comfort (COM) terms to operate on the realized trajectory.

sections.heading: What limits the teacher.
sections.text: On nuScenes, safety, on-road compliance, and comfort hold up across all four tiers—NC stays above 0.95 0.95 , DAC is saturated near 1.0 1.0 , TTC above 0.92 0.92 , and COM above 0.90 0.90 —so HD-PDMS never drops below 0.88 0.88 . There, the HD-Score is instead driven down almost entirely by route completion: R c R_{c} falls from 0.95 0.95 on Easy to 0.30 0.30 on Extreme, and because it multiplies the aggregate (Eq. 16 ), it alone pulls the Extreme HD-Score to 0.28 0.28 despite an HD-PDMS of 0.89 0.89 . On KITTI-360, drivable-area compliance also collapses (Extreme DAC 0.569 0.569 , HD-PDMS 0.354 0.354 ) and pulls the pooled Extreme HD-PDMS down to 0.767 0.767 . Even the privileged teacher cannot make progress on many Extreme scenarios, consistent with visually implausible initial configurations (e.g., other cars passing through each other) of the kind discussed in § 3.3 .

sections.text: We ablate the truncation rank of the structural loss. The headline uses k p = 13 k_{p}=13 , k r = 9 k_{r}=9 , the 80 % 80\% cumulative-energy cutoffs of the teacher spectra (§ 3.5 ). We compare it with half these ranks ( k p = 7 k_{p}=7 , k r = 5 k_{r}=5 ), twice these ranks ( k p = 26 k_{p}=26 , k r = 18 k_{r}=18 ), and a full-coordinate variant that skips the projection and matches the pairwise cosine-similarity matrix over all feature coordinates. Every variant keeps the rest of the recipe fixed: the same frozen teacher, the headline data including the 300 300 K HUGSim domain-adaptation frames, the action loss, λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , and the same training budget. All variants are evaluated with closed-loop HD-Score on all 436 436 HUGSim scenarios. Table 3 reports the results, and § 3.5 discusses why performance peaks at the spectrum cutoff.

sections.heading: B.2. Vision Backbone Ablation
sections.text: Figure 5 . Vision-backbone ablation. Closed-loop HD-Score under a fixed alignment recipe for each image backbone, trained on the headline data including the 300 300 K HUGSim domain-adaptation frames. We compare the selected DINOv3 backbone against the alternative image encoders DINOv2 and ResNet-50 under an identical alignment recipe: the same frozen teacher, the same paired frames, and the same adapter architecture and training budget; only the pretrained image encoder changes. The pretrained representation contributes measurably on top of the alignment objective: swapping it moves the closed-loop score from 0.499 0.499 (ResNet-50) and 0.512 0.512 (DINOv2) to 0.548 0.548 . The DINOv3 number matches the headline student of Table 8 ; the two baselines transfer the same adapter design onto a supervised ImageNet representation (ResNet-50) and an earlier self-supervised one (DINOv2). The ordering is consistent with what the frozen head consumes. The road and partner adapters are linear, so the head can only use the structure its input features already carry: a stronger pretrained representation enters the alignment already closer to the teacher’s feature geometry, and the linear adapters have less work left to do. The absolute gaps are modest, 0.049 0.049 between ResNet-50 and DINOv3, but they come entirely from the encoder swap, with the teacher, the data, and the recipe held fixed.

End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments. Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail; closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone. Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward. Our approach exploits this asymmetry by decoupling learning to drive and learning to plan from learning to see . We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action Kullback-Leibler divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss. Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on. From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard , above every published method including DriveZero-Scale ( 57.1 57.1 ), and 95.5 95.5 PDMS on navtest , without human demonstrations. 1. Introduction End-to-end autonomous driving maps raw sensor inputs ( e.g. , camera images) directly to control commands. Deep learning and large-scale driving data have made this approach widely adopted and continuously improved across benchmarks ( Bojarski et al., 2016 ; Codevilla et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ; Dauner et al., 2024a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . However, this progress relies on expensive standard pipelines that follow either of the two routes. The open-loop strategy draws its behavioral supervision from fleet logs: imitation copies logged human driving ( Codevilla et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ) , and open-loop reinforcement learning (RL) optimizes against logged trajectories ( Karkus et al., 2025 ) . These logs provide millions of multi-camera hours ( Caesar et al., 2020 ; Sun et al., 2020 ; Caesar et al., 2021 ) , yet safety-critical events (collisions, near-misses, recoveries, etc. ) remain vanishingly rare in natural driving: at NHTSA crash rates, a collision occurs only once every ∼ 16 {\sim}16 k driving hours ( National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 2025 ) , so logging a single rare event can easily cost over $1M in fleet operation alone ( Kelkar et al., 2025 ) . Each sub-route inherits this scarcity in its own way: imitation can only copy the actions the recorded drivers took, and open-loop RL never sees how other vehicles would have responded to the alternative actions it explores. Broadening interaction coverage with human data therefore demands ever more collection and curation. The closed-loop framework instead trains inside a photorealistic, sensor-rendering simulator ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ; Karkus et al., 2025 ) , where the policy experiences the consequences of its own actions. This interaction, however, costs rendering and a heavy vision-backbone forward pass at every step. Co-training multiple interacting agents multiplies these per-step costs, so most image-based closed-loop work instead trains the ego policy against scripted or log-replayed traffic, and the behavior distribution stays close to the logged or hand-designed content ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2022 ) . These costs confine this route to fine-tuning a pretrained imitation policy, as in Figure 1 , rather than pretraining driving competence from scratch. Recently, multi-agent self-play has risen as a promising alternative to offer the missing interaction: one shared policy controls every agent, so each policy improvement reshapes the traffic every other agent faces, and the interactive behavior co-evolves with the policy. Vectorized simulation makes this co-training highly efficient, executing millions of steps per second on commodity hardware ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2026 ; Seong et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Training requires only a basic definition of driving quality as per-step rewards: goal reaching, collision avoidance, comfort, and simple rule compliance. These rewards specify general driving objectives rather than separate rules for corner cases. The resulting interactions naturally produce the collisions, recoveries, yielding, negotiation, and overtaking that logged traffic seldom contains, all without expert trajectories or behavior-specific rewards. Despite its promise, however, self-play does not yield deployable end-to-end driving policies per se , as they observe vectorized scene state rather than raw sensors. Deploying these policies would require a two-stage perception stack that recovers their HD-map-style inputs from images. Such a stack demands high-quality perception, is sensitive to perception noise, and forfeits the co-optimization of a fully differentiable end-to-end model. As a result, it has mostly remained confined to traffic simulation rather than an end-to-end solution ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2026 ; Seong et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Konstantinidis et al., 2026 ; Ahmadi et al., 2026 ) . Conventional training pipeline vs. our reinforcement-learning pretraining pipeline. Conventional recipes imitate fleet logs and fine-tune on curated demonstrations, logged trajectories, or rendered simulation. They therefore need human data or rendering at every stage. Phase 1 (top right) trains a self-play policy π θ \pi_{\theta} with proximal policy optimization (PPO) in a multi-agent vectorized simulator. Phase 2 (middle right) freezes the policy as the self-play teacher and distills its rollouts into a trajectory teacher that also outputs a planned trajectory; both teachers read vector state. Phase 3 (bottom right) aligns an image-conditioned student to either frozen teacher: the self-play teacher yields the closed-loop student, and the trajectory teacher yields the planning student. The student keeps the teacher’s ego encoder unchanged and is not aligned on it; only the teacher’s scene features (road and partner, plus traffic for the trajectory teacher) enter the structural loss. An action loss matches the teacher’s action distribution, while a structural loss matches its pairwise relationships among scenes; for the planning student, an L2 loss also matches the plan the trajectory teacher selects among 16 16 samples. Alignment uses paired (image, scene-state) frames; it needs neither demonstrations nor online rendering during training. Blue modules are trainable; outlined modules are frozen. In the blue DINOv3 + Adapter block, only the adapter trains; the backbone stays frozen. The trajectory head and the L2 loss apply to the planning student only. In this work, we unite the strengths of self-play and end-to-end driving in a paradigm that learns driving policies without expert demonstrations. Self-play learns driving competence without human demonstrations but consumes vector state; end-to-end recipes consume raw sensors but depend on human demonstrations, whose coverage of rare interactions is the very gap identified above. We bridge this gap by decoupling learning to drive and learning to plan from learning to see , and we never use logged demonstration trajectories as supervision. Figure 1 contrasts its three stages with the conventional workflow. In the first stage, we train a policy π θ \pi_{\theta} tabula rasa through multi-agent self-play in TerraZero ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , our vectorized driving simulator, in the spirit of GigaFlow ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ) . One parameter set controls every agent in every scene. The policy learns from the long-tail distribution of its own behavior and never imitates a human trajectory. The resulting policy is a strong planner, scoring 94.19 94.19 on nuPlan val14 and 70.87 70.87 on the interactive long-tail InterPlan suite, above every imitation-based planner we are aware of, and 0.632 0.632 human-similarity on WOSAC 2023, on par with the strongest learned sim agents. In the second stage, the policy becomes the self-play teacher, and a trajectory teacher learns to plan from its self-play rollouts. A closed-loop policy emits one action per step, but planning interfaces and pseudo closed-loop benchmarks score a multi-second trajectory. We therefore distill the realized futures of these rollouts into the trajectory teacher through a flow-matching head. Like the self-play teacher, it still reads vector state. In the third stage, we freeze either teacher and align a vision student to it: the self-play teacher yields the closed-loop student, and the trajectory teacher yields the planning student. The student retains the teacher’s head unchanged and learns encoders that produce its scene features for road elements and surrounding agents from images instead of vector states; these encoders pair a pretrained vision backbone ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) with learned adapters supervised by paired (image, scene-state) frames of the same scene. The teacher’s per-state action distribution trains the student to choose the same actions. A feature-level structural loss preserves the teacher’s pairwise similarities among scene features, following the empirical finding that the teacher’s features are low-rank and redundant (§ 3.5 ). For the planning student, a trajectory loss also matches the plan the trajectory teacher selects among 16 16 samples, so the student learns the selection and needs none at test time. The closed-loop and planning students are two interfaces of one self-play teacher, and neither sees a human trajectory. Our framework preserves the naturalistic driving competence learned through self-play. On photorealistic closed-loop benchmarks, the closed-loop student attains an aggregate HD-Score of 0.548 0.548 , exceeding every published end-to-end baseline on every HUGSim dataset split (Table 1 ). Likewise, on NAVSIM, the planning student reaches 59.4 59.4 EPDMS on the NAVSIMv2 navhard split, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale ( 57.1 57.1 ), and 95.5 95.5 PDMS on the NAVSIMv1 navtest split, above every published sensor-based method (Table 2 ). TerraTransfer++ extends our earlier TerraTransfer report ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) with trajectory distillation, the second stage. The cost of learning to drive moves upstream into self-play. This one-time compute is efficient and reusable. The self-play policy is trained in 96 hours on 16 A100 GPUs, covering over 2.4B kilometers of simulated driving without human demonstrations. It can then supervise a range of vision frontends, alignment datasets, sensor stacks, and downstream specializations. During alignment, the vision encoder’s only teacher signals are the frozen head’s per-state action distribution, the teacher’s scene-feature relations, and, for the planning student, the trajectory teacher’s selected plan; all three derive from the self-play teacher’s behavior and are computed on a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames. No expert behavior is required anywhere. Any retained perception labels are policy-agnostic and reusable across frontends. They are obtainable offline through auto-labeling, which separates this requirement from the demonstration-collection burden of behavior cloning. In our case, the encoder is aligned over 1.83 1.83 M paired nuPlan frames plus 300 300 K HUGSim domain-adaptation frames on 8 A100 GPUs in 10 hours. The nuPlan paired frames are logged real camera images and the domain-adaptation frames are rendered once offline, so training needs no online rendering; rendering in the loop would be roughly 6,000 × 6{,}000\times slower than vector rollout ( 175 175 k vs. 30 30 fps across all cameras). We make the following contributions: • A novel demonstration-free paradigm for learning end-to-end driving policies. A policy π θ \pi_{\theta} first learns to drive through multi-agent self-play in a vectorized simulator. Its per-state action distributions then supervise encoders that produce the policy’s scene features from images, with no logged-trajectory supervision at any stage. • Trajectory distillation from self-play. A flow-matching trajectory teacher learns the realized futures of the self-play teacher’s rollouts, and the same alignment recipe plus a loss on the teacher’s selected plan transfers it to a camera-only planner (§ 2.3 and § 2.4 ). The planner reaches 59.4 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2 navhard , above every published method including DriveZero-Scale ( 57.1 57.1 ), and 95.5 95.5 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 navtest , above every published sensor-based method (Table 2 ). • A feature-level structural alignment mechanism. We align the encoder directly with the teacher’s pooled scene features instead of cascading reconstruction and detection. A batch-relational low-rank structural loss matches the pairwise scene similarities induced by the teacher. • Demonstration-free closed-loop driving beyond published imitation-based end-to-end methods. On photorealistic closed-loop scenarios in HUGSim, the camera-based closed-loop student, aligned to a teacher that never observed a human demonstration, outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method (Table 1 ). 2. Method We first train a vector-state teacher through self-play, then distill its rollouts into a trajectory teacher that also plans, and finally align a vision student to either teacher with structural and action losses. 2.1. TerraZero: Self-Play Vectorized Simulator Self-play runs in TerraZero ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , a vectorized driving simulator that compiles nuPlan high-definition (HD) maps into static lane topology, lane boundaries, and drivable-area geometry. Training uses no nuPlan logged trajectories, logged agent initial states, logged goals, human actions, or replayed traffic. Instead, controlled vehicles spawn procedurally from lane centerlines through rejection sampling. This procedure produces collision-free, drivable initial scenes. Each controlled vehicle receives a procedural goal between 20 20 and 100 100 m ahead along the reachable lane graph. Reaching a goal triggers another sample from the same topology. The simulator also places vulnerable road users and static obstacles as scene context. The learned policy controls vehicles only. Appendix A.1.1 gives the complete environment and training configuration. At each 0.1 0.1 s step, a vehicle observes its ego kinematics and goal signal, nearby road polylines and traffic controls, and neighboring scene entities. Each entity includes relative pose, velocity, heading, size, type, and validity. These three input groups become the ego, road, and partner streams used by the teacher below. Appendix A.1.2 specifies the observation vectors. Appendices A.1.3 – A.1.5 detail rewards and dynamics. 2.2. Self-Play Pretraining: The Teacher Setup. We pretrain a driving policy π θ \pi_{\theta} through self-play in TerraZero. A single set of parameters θ \theta controls all agents in every scene. We pool their transitions into one on-policy buffer. Each agent’s “surrounding traffic” consists of other instances of the current policy. The multi-agent interaction distribution therefore evolves with the policy itself. Policy architecture. At each step, an agent observes its own ego state o t e o^{e}_{t} . This state contains its kinematics, its goal signal, and the per-episode reward-weight vector w ( n ) w^{(n)} introduced below. Trajectory Distillation The frozen teacher π θ T \pi^{T}_{\theta} emits one action per step but publishes no planned trajectory, which planning interfaces and pseudo closed-loop protocols require. We therefore give it a second interface: we distill its rollouts into a trajectory teacher that also outputs a plan (Phase 2 of Fig. 1 ). Both teachers read privileged vector state; § 2.4 turns either into a vision policy. Target construction. For each frame of a self-play rollout, the trajectory target is the realized future of π θ T \pi^{T}_{\theta} , not a logged human trajectory. We record the next 80 80 ego poses at the native 10 10 Hz control rate ( 8 8 s), each expressed in the current ego frame as forward offset, lateral offset, and heading change, and standardize every timestep and dimension with dataset statistics. A possible bridge is a cascade : a perception module recovers the teacher’s vector inputs (bounding boxes, lane polylines, and partner kinematics) from the image, and the frozen teacher then consumes these recovered inputs. Experiments We test one claim: vision policies distilled from a self-play teacher can drive competitively in closed loop and plan competitively in pseudo closed loop. No training stage touches a logged human trajectory. We first define the setup and the two scorers (§ 3.1 ) and present the self-play teacher that anchors the pipeline (§ 3.2 ); the teacher sets the reference level. We then compare the student and the teacher against end-to-end baselines on every HUGSim split and against concurrent self-play-to-pixel systems on their 345 345 -scenario protocol (§ 3.3 ), and compare the trajectory student against published planners on NAVSIM (§ 3.4 ); the two students are the main results. Next, the insights and ablations of § 3.5 show that, under matched data and compute, self-play alignment outperforms imitation and a modular cascade: the training paradigm sets the score, both alignment losses are necessary and nearly lossless, and the low-rank structural target is read from the teacher’s spectrum rather than tuned. Setup We evaluate on all 436 436 scenarios of HUGSim ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , a photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark, spanning its four dataset splits (nuScenes 88 88 , PandaSet 127 127 , KITTI-360 113 113 , Waymo 108 108 ), each divided into Easy, Medium, Hard, and Extreme tiers. On HUGSim we report two scores throughout: the closed-loop (CL) HD-Score, which scores the realized rollout, and HUGSim’s native scorer, which scores a planned trajectory. Our single-step controller replans at each step, emitting one immediate jerk action that we Euler-integrate into HUGSim’s bicycle-model control signals in causal closed form, without a second dynamics model (Appendix A.1.5 specifies the conversion). The closed-loop scorer executes only this first action per step and scores the resulting rollout.
